newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Focus-Ericsson thumbs nose at Sweden.
newsitem.headline: Focus-Ericsson thumbs nose at Sweden.

text.p: Mobile phone giant Ericsson, in a singularly unScandinavian gesture, thumbed its nose at the Swedish government on Tuesday and said it was moving a small subsidiary out of Sweden.

The decision, bound to infuriate the centre-left government, was announced after Prime Minister Goran Persson took on Ericsson, accusing chief executive Lars Ramqvist of playing politics by criticising the business climate in Sweden.
Hours later, Ericsson released a one-page statement announcing its Transport and Cable Networks unit's headquarters was moving to Britain from Sweden.

"The reason for the move...is to create a new improved business climate to strengthen Ericsson's position. In addition the change will lower the unit's cost levels in the longer term and facilitate the process of finding.

"With the move we want to create a new winning business climate within this part of Ericsson's business. The conditions to achieve this will be much better in a new environment," said Rory Buckley, head of the subsidiary.
Ericsson joined a growing chorus of companies at the weekend who say a poor business climate and crushing taxation may force them to move operations overseas.
In a radio interview, Ramqvist said the company board had decided to look into a possible move of the Stockholm head office.
"The investigation should be seen in the light that only three percent of our business is in Sweden," Ramqvist told the radio.
"For tax reasons it is almost hopeless to get a foreigner to move here," Ramqvist told the radio. Highly paid employees routinely pay 60 percent of their salaries in tax.
"If politicians don't understand that we must reward development and competence, Ericsson won't manage the restructuring we are facing," Ramqvist said.
Persson, head of a centre-left Social Democratic government that for years has had a prickly relationship with the country's powerful business leaders, accused them of playing politics.

He said some of the companies threatening to quit Sweden had been regularly posting record profits. "I don't quite get it if this success is supposed to be an example of how bad the business climate is," Persson said.

"I could have understood it when interest rates were at 500 percent (during a 1992 financial crisis) but not now when we have state finances in order and companies are making big profits. I don't know what they base their arguments on," he added.
Persson said an article in a newspaper in which 100 managing directors slammed the government's decision to phase out nuclear power was a case in point of business leaders playing politics.
Junior Finance Minister Thomas Ostros, who deals with taxation issues, rejected Ericsson's complaints in a newspaper article on Tuesday, saying the corporate climate in Sweden was exceptionally good.
"Where else can they find a country with the kind of labour force we have, with labour market stability, with little bureaucracy and in addition get low mortgages?" Ostros said.
Neighbouring Finland and other European countries have special tax rules for foreigners.
Persson hinted at a compromise by saying he was looking at tax relief for key foreign employees working in Sweden.
Ericsson employs about 90,000 people in 130 countries. Tuesday's announcement affected only about 70 people.
-- Simon Haydon, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1004
